segments.text: For every OOP concept below, keep asking what design purpose the syntax is actually serving, rather than treating each feature as an isolated language rule — abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism are four distinct design ideas, and connecting each language feature back to the specific one it implements is what separates real understanding from surface memorization.

Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects that combine state (data) and behaviour (functions that act on that data) together into one unit. Abstraction means showing only the essential features of something while hiding unnecessary internal detail — a driver uses a steering wheel and pedals without needing to understand the engine’s internals, and a well-designed class works the same way. Encapsulation is the specific mechanism that enforces this hiding: it controls access to an object’s internal state, protecting its invariants (conditions that must always remain true) from being broken by uncontrolled external interference. A class defines a type — the blueprint — and an object is one concrete instance created from that blueprint; data members store an object’s state, and member functions operate on that state. Example: a BankAccount object may expose deposit() and withdraw() as its public interface, while keeping the actual balance field itself protected from arbitrary external modification, so that every legitimate change to the balance is forced to go through validated logic.

Static members belong to the class itself, shared across every instance, rather than belonging to any one individual object — a static counter, for instance, can track how many objects of a class have been created in total, since that count is a property of the class as a whole, not of any single object. Composition means one object contains another as one of its own members, modeling a “has-a” relationship. Example: a Car class can contain an Engine object as one of its data members — this is composition, and it is a genuinely different relationship from inheritance (which models “is-a”, covered in Section C). The this keyword, in languages like C++, refers to the current object a member function is operating on, which is what lets the same function body work correctly across many different object instances. const helps express data or functions that are guaranteed not to change under the language’s rules, which both documents intent and lets the compiler catch accidental modifications. friend access is a controlled, explicit exception to a class’s normal access restrictions, granted deliberately to specific outside functions or classes — it should never be confused with inheritance, since a friend gains access without becoming a subtype of the class at all.

Operator overloading lets selected operators work naturally with user-defined types while keeping their ordinary, familiar meaning for the language’s built-in types. Example: a Complex number class can define + so that writing c1 + c2 naturally produces a new complex number representing their sum, exactly as + already works for ordinary integers. Overloading should improve code readability by letting natural notation apply to new types — it never creates entirely new operators, and it never changes an operator’s precedence or associativity rules.

Inheritance creates a new class from an existing one so that common behaviour can be reused and then specialized further. Example: Vehicle can serve as a base class, with Car inheriting Vehicle’s common properties while adding car-specific behaviour of its own. Single inheritance derives from exactly one base class; multiple inheritance derives from more than one simultaneously. Overriding replaces an inherited behaviour with a derived class’s own implementation of the same interface — this is genuinely different from overloading (Section C’s first half), which is a compile-time choice between multiple versions of an operator or function name, whereas overriding is resolved through the object’s actual type at runtime (covered fully in Section D). A key design discipline: inheritance should model a genuine “is-a” relationship (a Car really is a kind of Vehicle); when the relationship is really “has-a” instead, composition (Section B) is the more appropriate tool, and reaching for inheritance where composition actually fits is a common and costly design mistake.

Polymorphism means a single interface can represent genuinely different concrete behaviours depending on the actual object involved. In C++, this is commonly implemented at runtime through virtual functions: a call made through a base-class pointer or reference can dispatch, at runtime, to whichever derived class’s implementation actually matches the real object being pointed to. Example: a Shape base class may declare an area() function, with Circle and Rectangle each implementing it differently according to their own geometry; a collection of Shape references can then call area() on every element uniformly, without the calling code needing to know each object’s concrete type in advance — this is exactly the power polymorphism provides. A pure virtual function (one with no implementation in the base class at all) makes that class abstract: it defines a required interface but can never be instantiated directly, only used as a base for concrete derived classes. The essential distinction worth tracing carefully: overloading is a compile-time choice between different functions or operators sharing the same name, based on the arguments provided; overriding and virtual dispatch are resolved at runtime, based on the actual type of the object behind a pointer or reference — confusing these two mechanisms is one of the most common conceptual errors in this whole topic.

blocks.text: E. Standard Template Library, Files, and Exceptions

segments.text: The standard template library (STL) provides reusable, pre-built containers, iterators, and algorithms, precisely so that common data-structure and algorithmic needs do not need to be reimplemented from scratch in every program. Common STL containers include vector (a dynamically resizable array), list (a linked structure), map (associates keys with values), and set (stores unique elements); common algorithms include sorting and searching routines that work generically across these containers. Example: a vector can grow dynamically as elements are added and be sorted directly using a library sorting algorithm, rather than writing a new sort routine every single time a program needs one.

Streams provide a consistent model for input and output, treating a keyboard, a file, or another data source or destination through the same general interface. Sequential files are processed strictly in order from beginning to end; random-access files instead allow the program to jump directly to a specific position, where the underlying language and file system support this. Exceptions separate error signalling cleanly from a program’s ordinary return-value flow, commonly implemented through a try/throw/catch pattern: code that might fail is placed in a try block, an error condition is signalled by throwing an exception object, and a matching catch block handles that specific error type separately from the program’s normal logic. Managing resources correctly around exceptions — making sure files are closed and memory is released even when an error occurs partway through — is an essential and frequently tested discipline in this area.

Object-Oriented Programming key takeaways: abstraction hides unnecessary detail; encapsulation is the specific access-control mechanism that enforces that hiding. Composition (“has-a”) and inheritance (“is-a”) solve different design problems and should not be substituted for each other. Operator overloading is a compile-time convenience for readable notation; it never creates new operators or changes precedence. Overloading and overriding are resolved at fundamentally different times — compile-time for overloading, runtime for virtual-function overriding and polymorphism — and this timing difference is the crux of nearly every exam question that tests the distinction. The STL, streams, and exceptions all exist for the same underlying reason: to let programmers reuse well-tested, well-understood solutions to common problems rather than reinventing them under time pressure.
